Cellulose Solubility in Deep Eutectic Solvents: Inspecting Quantitative Hydrogen-Bonding Analysis

Kuang-Jie Xuª,b, Bao-Qing Zhangª,b*, Xin Qiaoª, and Chen-Yang Liuª,b* ª CAS Key Laboratory of Engineering Plastics, Beijing National Laboratory for Molecular Sciences, Institute of Chemistry, the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China b University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, China
Electronic Supplementary Information

Abstract According to the Kamlet-Abraham-Taft (KAT) polarity parameters (α, β, π*), polymers and solvents can be categorized as hydrogen-bond (H-bond) acidic (α>β) or H-bond basic (α<β). Recently, we proposed a quantitative hydrogen bonding (QHB) analysis to predict the solubility of polymers in ionic liquids (ILs) using the product of ΔαΔβ<0 as an indicator, where Δα is the difference between the H-bond acidic parameters of the polymer and IL, and Δβ is the difference in their basicity, while the prerequisite of the "complementary" principle (i.e., that one component is H-bond acidic and the other is basic) is satisfied. Here, the applicability of QHB analysis was first confirmed by testing the solubilities of carefully chosen polymer/deep eutectic solvent (DES) pairs, as the DESs were eutectic mixtures dominated by hydrogen bonding interactions. Then, our attention focused on the solubility of cellulose in DESs. Our testing results as well as the typical published results were summarized, which indicate that the potential DESs for cellulose dissolution and regeneration must be of the H-bond basic type because the "complementary" principle should be satisfied as a prerequisite. However, the H-bond basic DESs investigated in this study do not show the superior solubility of cellulose that has been commonly observed for H-bond basic ILs, even if the criterion of ΔαΔβ<0 is satisfied for both DESs and ILs. Possible reasons for this discrepancy are given to understand the varying effectiveness in cellulose dissolution for H-bond basic DESs and ILs.
**Keywords** Deep eutectic solvent; Cellulose dissolution; Empirical polarity parameters; Hydrogen bonding interaction

**Citation:** Xu, K. J.; Zhang, B. Q.; Qiao, X.; Liu, C. Y. Cellulose solubility in deep eutectic solvents: inspecting quantitative hydrogen-bonding analysis. *Chinese J. Polym. Sci.* **2023**, *41*, 75–83.

# INTRODUCTION Polymer dissolution in solvents is always an important area attracting considerable interest from researchers in polymer science and engineering because in many applications, polymers are directly utilized or further modified/processed in the form of solution. [1-3] Knowledge about the physical chemistry of polymer solutions is also an important theme for the foundation of polymer science. [4] Currently, many physical parameters of polymers still have to be characterized using their solutions, such as measuring the molecular weight and molecular weight distribution using gel permeation chromatography (GPC) and detecting the branching lever of polyolefins using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy.
It is well accepted that Flory-Huggins theory for dilute solutions (Eq. 1) is the cornerstone to understand and predict the solvation process for polymers and the phase behavior of

$\Delta G_m = - T\Delta S_m + \Delta H_m$ $=kT(\phi_s \ln\phi_s + \frac{\phi_p}{N_p}\ln\phi_p) + kT(\chi\phi_p \phi_s)$ (1)

where φs and φp are the volume fractions of solvent and polymer, respectively; Np is the ratio of the molar volume of polymer to that of solvent and is proportional to the degree of polymerization; χ is called the Flory-Huggins interaction parameter, which is proportional to (δp – δs)²/RT, and δp and δs are the so-called Hildebrand solubility parameters for polymer and solvent, respectively. During the dissolving process for the polymer, the entropy change (ΔSm>0) always favors the mixing of the polymer and solvent, but its value is usually small, and the free energy change is mainly controlled by the enthalpy term. An effective interaction parameter χeff can be adopted to account for the nonideality of real polymer solutions.[5] When χeff<0, the enthalpy item also favors the dissolution of the polymer in the selected solvent. If there is a way to predict the sign of χeff, the solubility of a polymer/solvent pair can be forecast.

(QHB) analysis method to access and help to predict the solu- bility of polymers in room-temperature ionic liquids (ILs).[6] This method is based on the Kamlet-Abraham-Taft (KAT) po- larity parameters, which have been extensively used for cha- racterizing different types of solute/solvent interactions.[7-9] The KAT polarity parameters in a simplified form of linear solvation energy relationship (LSER) is given by:[10]

(XYZ) = (XYZ)₀ + sπ* + aα + bβ (2) where (XYZ) is the solvent-dependent physico-chemical property determined for a variety of solvents, (XYZ)₀ is the same property for a reference medium (e.g., gas phase or inert solvent), α, denoting the hydrogen-bond (H-bond) donating ability or acidity, β, denoting the H-bond accepting ability or basicity, π*, a mixed parameter representing the polarizability and dipolarity, s, a, and b are solvent-independent coefficients reflecting the related influence of the π*-, α-, and β-components, respectively, upon (XYZ). The polarity parameters, α, β, and π*, are usually obtained using the so-called solvatochromic comparison method. [9,11,12] Polymers and ILs can be categorized as either H-bond acidic (α>β) or H-bond basic (α<β). First, the "complementary" requirement, i.e., one H-bond acidic component and another basic component, must be fulfilled to dissolve the polymer in a selected IL. Then, if the product of ΔαΔβ<0, where Δα = αp - αIL, and Δβ = βp - βIL, the IL usually exhibits satisfying solubility for the tested polymer. Strictly speaking, the change of hydrogen bonding interaction energy for the dissolving of polymer in an IL should be (Aαpβp + BαpβIL) - (CαILβp + DαILβIL), where A, B, C and D are coefficients according to Eq. (2). [10] However, the good correlation of ΔαΔβ = -[(αILβp + αpβIL) - (αpβp + αILβIL)] < 0 and the solubility of polymer/IL mixtures suggests that the simplified relationship, (αILβp + αpβIL) - (αpβp + αILβIL), can be used to approximately predict the change of hydrogen bonding interaction energy for the mixing of polymer/IL, i.e., ΔαΔβ<0 generally indicates that the hydrogen bonding interaction energy between the polymer and IL is higher than the hydrogen bonding interaction energy inside the components themselves. Because nonspecific (van der Waals) and polar interactions are commonly weaker than hydrogen bonding interactions in polymer/IL mixtures, QHB analysis (ΔαΔβ) provides a simple but reliable way to predict the sign of ΔHₘ (i.e., Xeff), and thus the solubility of a polymer/IL mixture.

Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are eutectic mixtures, typic-ally composed of hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs, e.g., qua-ternary ammonium salts, and aromatic alcohols) and hydro-gen bond donors (HBDs, e.g., carboxylic acids, amides, amines, and polyols) at certain stoichiometric ratios.[13–15] They are considered as "designer" solvents that are alterna-tives to ILs because they also exhibit negligible vapor pres-sures at room temperature, and their physico-chemical prop-erties can be fine-tuned by varying the starting HBA and HBD components or simply altering their molar ratios. They have extra advantages compared with ILs; for example, they do not need any solvent and special purification steps during syn-thesis, and they usually have low toxicity and cost, as the raw materials for preparation are usually nontoxic and abundant.[16] DESs, as new-generation solvents, show applica-tion potential in many fields of polymer sciences, such as polymer polymerization,[17] biomass fractionation,[18] and ion-

ic soft materials. [19] Most of these applications involve the dis-solution of polymers in desired DESs. It is well accepted that hydrogen bonding plays an important role in the depression of melting points for HBA and HBD components and the formation of DESs. On that account, it is believed that the QHB analysis developed for polymer/IL mixtures can also work well for predicting the solubility of polymers in DESs.

Here, the validity of QHB analysis was first evaluated by testing the solubility of carefully selected polymer/DES pairs. Then, attention was given to the solubility of cellulose in DESS because most DESs adopted to dissolve cellulose materials actually show no or very limited solubilities. [20-22] The QHB analysis based on hydrogen bonding interactions can provide a rational explanation.

# RESULTS AND DISCUSSION ## Evaluating the Applicability of QHB Analysis for Polymer/DES Mixtures First, the applicability of QHB analysis for polymer/DES mixtures is evaluated by testing the solubilities of seven typical polymers in carefully selected DESs. The details about the polymers used in this study are provided in the electronic supplementary information (ESI). The investigated polymers are listed in Table S1 (in ESI) with the chemical structure and the KAT parameters (α, β, π") for each polymer. According to the relative sizes of the α and β values, the seven polymers can be categorized as H-bond basic or H-bond acidic polymers. It should be noted that the α values of H-bond basic polymers are zero or near zero, indicating that there are more electronegative functional groups in these polymers, which commonly act as proton acceptors in forming hydrogen bonds. [23] Correspondingly, nine DESs are chosen to pair with these polymers to prepare solutions. Similarly, the DESs can also be categorized into H-bond acidic DESs (Nos. 1–4 in Table 1) or basic DESs (Nos. 7–9 in Table 1). Unlike ILs, some DESs have almost the same α and β values that can be called H-bond neutral DESs (Nos. 5 and 6 in Table 1). Noted that the DESs investigated here are all the type III DESs without the component of metal halides, [13] as there might exist different types of interactions between polymers and metal ions other than hydrogen bonding interaction for the other three types of DESs. Moreover, the DESs are selected mainly based on their α and β values. We try to keep the β values invariant, while make the α values gradually change in a relatively wide range for the selected H-bond acidic and H-bond basic DESs, respectively. The chemical structures of the HBA and HBD components used to synthesize these DESs are given in Fig. 1. The hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity for every DES according to its solubility in water is also provided in Table 1. However, the hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity does not show any distinct influence on the solubilities of the investigated polymer/DES mixtures according to the solubility testing results, as discussed below. The experimental details about the preparation of DESs, and the dissolution conditions of the selected polymers in these DESs can be found in ESI.

Poly(vinyl pyrrolidone) (PVP) possesses the highest β value among the selected H-bond basic polymers (Table S1 in ESI). It can be dissolved by both H-bond acidic and H-bond neu- tral DESs no matter they are hydrophilic or hydrophobic, but it is insoluble in all the H-bond basic DESs used in this study,

even when the criterion of ΔαΔβ<0 is satisfied (Table S2 in ESI). Two other H-bond basic polymers, polyethylene oxide (PEO) and polyvinyl acetate (PVAc), are also insoluble in the H-bond basic DESs. Additionally, they are not soluble in the selected H-bond neutral DESs. For PVAc, this can be ascribed to both Δα and Δβ being less than zero, and the fact that ΔαΔβ<0 requirement is not satisfied. However, for PEO, its insolubility in the DESs formed by ChCl with GlyA and LevA, respectively, does not satisfy the criterion of ΔαΔβ<0, as (Δα, Δβ) are (-0.49, 0.15) and (-0.51, 0.08) for two PEO/DES pairs. It can be found that the two Δβ values are relatively small. Considering that the used KAT parameters are adopted from different references and are obtained by using different solvatochromic probes, an uncertainty of 0.1 or even more for KAT parameters is very possible. [11] This is an unavoidable limitation of the solvatochromic comparison method. The accuracy of the QHB analysis is mainly determined by the accuracy of KAT parameters adopted. As a suggestion, it is better to use KAT parameters measured using the same sets of solvatochromic probes to ensure the predictive accuracy of QHB analysis. Taking the possible uncertainties of KAT parameters into account, the insolubility of PEO in these two solvents is acceptable even as the QHB analysis predicts the solubility. On the other hand, for all the tested H-bond acidic polymer/H-bond acidic DES pairs, none are soluble regardless of whether or not the criterion of ΔαΔβ<0 is satisfied. All these results suggest that the "complementary" principle of solubility (one

component H-bond acidic and the other basic) we have previ- ously found in polymer/IL mixtures [6] is also well applicable for the polymer/DES mixtures studied here, while the H-bond neutral DESs can be considered to exhibit duality, i.e., they can be treated as either H-bond acidic or H-bond basic.

For all 13 pairs of H-bond basic polymer/H-bond acidic DES examined here (Table S2 in ESI), only two pairs violate the proposed ΔαΔβ criterion. One is PEO/ChCl-EG (insoluble), and the other is PVAc/menthol-LevA (soluble). The values of (Δα, Δβ) for the two mixtures are (-1.47, 0.08) (soluble as predicted) and (-1.56, -0.18) (insoluble as predicted), respectively. The failure to predict solubility can also be ascribed to the uncertainty in the adopted KAT parameters.

When we tried to seek H-bond basic DESs, it was found that they are evidently less than the H-bond acidic DESs. In a typical DES, the molar percentage of the HBD component is commonly equal to or higher than that of HBA. Moreover, the HBA component is usually an organic salt, which can also be considered to be composed of HBA (anion) and HBD (cation) components. Thus, there are more functional groups inside a DES that can play the role of proton donors, and thus, it is prone to exhibit as H-bond acidic, which embodies a relatively high α value. Although some research works have been carried out to systemically study the influence of the types, chemical structures, and molar ratios of HBA and HBD on the polarities of different families of DESs, a general and detailed delineation has not been obtained at present. The synthetic H-bond acidic polymers tested here, poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) and poly(2-hydroxyethyl methac- rylate) (PHEMA), can be easily dissolved by H-bond basic DESs (dissolved polymer concentration ≥2.0 wt%) when the cri- terion of ΔΑΔΒ<0 is well met. For microcrystalline cellulose (MCC), the situation is quite different. It is well known that cel- lulose is difficult to dissolve due to the strong intra- and inter- molecular interactions between cellulose chains and the res- ulting high degree of crystallinity. [29] Both the high Α (1.31) and Β (0.62) values of MCC suggest the strength of the hydro- gen bonding interactions inside cellulose macromolecules. For the three H-bond basic DESs listed in Table 1, only the DES of MeaCI-DETA (1:4) shows a distinct dissolving capacity for MCC. It can dissolve more than 2.0 wt% MCC after being heated at 110 °C for 24 h. Less than 0.2 wt% MCC can be dis- solved by the other two TBAB-based DESs under the same conditions, although they should have considerable dissolv- ing ability according to the (ΔΑ, ΔΒ) values obtained for mix- tures of MCC and TBAB-based DESs (Table S2 in ESI). More dis- cussions about the solubility of cellulose in various DESs will be given in the next section.

## Solubilities of Cellulose in DESs Looking for solvents for cellulose is an important task in the fields of research and application of cellulose because cellulose materials usually have to be dissolved for characterization, modification, and processing. [3,30,31] A successful solvent or solvent system should be able to effectively break the strong intra- and inter-molecular hydrogen bonding interactions in cellulose. For the KAT parameters of cellulose, both the α (1.31) and β (0.62) values are very high, and α>β at the same time. According to the criterion of ΔαΔβ<0, the potential solvents should be strong H-bond basic solvents with β values larger than that of cellulose.

In the past, many studies have been carried out to develop and evaluate efficient DES solvents for cellulose and to scru- tinize the dissolution mechanism.[20,21,32,33] However, most DESs adopted in these studies are indeed H-bond acidic DESs, which show no or very limited solubility for cellulose materi- als, as listed in the upper part of Table 2, including many ChCl-based DESs reported in the literature.

We also selected four H-bond acidic DESs to test their dis- solving capacities for MCC (c.f., Table 1 and Table S2 in ESI). There was no sign of the dissolution of MCC with a concentra- tion of 0.2 wt% in these DESs after the MCC/DES mixtures were heated at 110 °C for 24 h. The white MCC powders in the mixtures settled down very quickly to the bottom of the glass bottles after the stirring was stopped (Fig. S1 in ESI). Moreover, the light-yellow colors observed for some mixtures, such as those in Figs. S1(b) and S1(d) (in ESI), are due to the solvents themselves and are not caused by the long-time heating or dissolution of cellulose.

TBAB-AP, as a kind of H-bond basic DES, were picked to study their dissolving capacity for H-bond acidic polymers. PVA and PHEMA showed good solubilities (≥2.0 wt%) in TBAB-AP DESs with molar ratios of both 1:2 and 1:4, which conformed to the prediction of QHB analysis very well. However, MCC with a concentration of 0.2 wt% was only par- tially dissolved in both solvents even after being heated at 110 °C for 24 h (Figs. 3a and 3b). The mixture of 0.2 wt% MCC/ТВАВ-АР (1:4) was observed using a polarized optical microscope (POM) before and after heating (Fig. S2 in ESI). It is obvious that most of the crystallized MCC particles disap- pear, but bright dots or areas are still observed indicating the insoluble particles. The photos verify that MCC can be par- tially dissolved in TBAB-AP (1:4). The results obtained from POM observation are similar to those obtained for the other three DESs based on tetrabutylammonium halite listed in Fig. 3.

As chloride anions can form stronger hydrogen bonds with the proton donors than bromide anions, we further prepared TBACI-AP DESs with molar ratios of both 1:2 and 1:4 (Table 2) to determine the influence of varying the anion of the HBA component. However, 0.2 wt% MCC could not be completely dissolved in TBACI-AP DESs either. All the solutions were opaque and had somewhat light-yellow colors, and their vis- cosities increased evidently. As shown in Fig. 3, the unsolved but swollen MCC particles were suspended in the solvents and did not settle after the magnetic stirring was stopped. The as-prepared DESs were observed to be transparent and colorless, so it was conjectured that the colors of MCC solu- tions are due to the dissolution of cellulose. The DESs with a molar ratio of 1:4 are more capable of dissolving cellulose than the corresponding DESs with a molar ratio of 1:2, as the yellow colors are slightly deeper for the former (Fig. 3b versus Fig. 3a for TBAB-AP, and Fig. 3d versus Fig. 3c for TBACI-AP).

This solvent attracted our attention because it has two sets of KAT parameters in the lit- erature, (1.41, 0.99, 0.76)[12] versus (0.84, 1.19, 0.80),[37] which

indicates that it is either H-bond acidic or basic. Its mixture with 0.2 wt% MCC exhibits a very similar appearance to that of other H-bond acidic DESs in dissolving MCC. The MCC powders were not dissolved, and they also settled at the bottom of the solvent after thermal dissolution was stopped (Fig. S1e, in ESI). This result indicates that TBACI-OctA (1:2) is indeed a H-bond acidic DES. This is reasonable considering the difference in hydrogen bond donating abilities between AP and OctA. [12]

## Similarities and Differences between the Dissolution of Cellulose in DESs and ILs The survey carried out here and other typical published results for investigating the solubilities of cellulose in different DESs and ILs, including the dissolving conditions used, are summarized in Table 2. According to all the results summarized in Table 2, it can be said that the potential solvents for cellulose dissolution and regeneration must be H-bond basic solvents for both DESs and ILs because the "complementary" principle, as a prerequisite, should be satisfied.

These strategies were also used to study their influ- ences on the solubilities of cellulose for the H-bond basic DESs investigated in this study. Additionally, it is worth noting that cellulose/IL solutions and many synthetic polymer/IL solutions usually show con- centration-dependent indices for the specific viscosity (ηsp) of 1, 2, and 14/3 in dilute, semi-dilute, and concentrated re- gimes, respectively, which is the power law for a neutral poly- mer in θ-solvent, as predicted by the scaling theory.[41] Re- cently, Liu et al. reported that for the solutions of cellulose/DES of choline hydroxide (ChOH)–urea (1:2), the scaling values were 0.54, 1.47, and 3.21 in three regimes, which closely follow the power laws of 1/2, 3/2, and 15/4 ob- tained for salt-free polyelectrolyte solutions.[34] It should be noted that the ChOH–urea DES used to prepare cellulose solu- tions is an aqueous system with a water content of 11.8 wt%. More experimental results are needed to explore this topic in the future.
## CONCLUSIONS The applicability of the newly developed QHB analysis based on the KAT polarity parameters for polymer/DES (the type III)

was evaluated by testing the solubility of carefully selected polymer/DES pairs. The DES systems were chosen because it was generally accepted that hydrogen bonding interactions play an important role in the formation of DESs. Based on the dissolution results for all the tested polymer/DES pairs, it is concluded that (1) the "complementary" principle (one component H-bond acidic and the other basic) as a prerequisite has to be satisfied if a polymer can be expected to be dissolved in a desired DES. The "complementary" principle can help one to understand why many DESs exhibit very limited or no solubilities for cellulose materials in previous studies. This is because most of the DESs adopted in these studies have been of the H-bond acidic type. It is not surprising that cellulose, which is a kind of strong H-bond acidic polymer, cannot be dissolved in H-bond acidic DESs. (2) The QHB analysis works well for predicting the solubility of polymers in DESs. The H-bond basic DESs, which satisfy the criterion of ΔαΔβ<0, exhibit positive capacities for cellulose dissolution. The DES of MeaCl-DETA (1:4) can dissolve MCC at concentrations ranging between 2.0 wt% and 3.0 wt%. However, the superior solubility of cellulose (≥10 wt%), which is very common for typical H-bond basic ILs, is rarely observed for H-bond basic DESs. Two possible reasons for this are proposed: the number of hydrogen bonds formed between cellulose-DESs is less than that between cellulose-ILs, and the entropy gain for the dissolution of cellulose in ILs is higher than that for the dissolution process in DESs.

In the future, more research is needed to delineate the in- fluences of the types, chemical structures, and molar ratios of HBA and HBD species on the KAT polarities of DESs. The first- principle-based COSMO-RS derived modeling approach has also been used to predict the KAT polarity scales of DESs.[45] It is believed that all these efforts will help to rapidly screen effi- cient DESs with the guidance of QHB analysis for the dissolu- tion of a specific polymer, including natural polymers, such as cellulose, lignin, chitin, and starch.

[1-3] Knowledge about the physical chemistry of polymer solutions is also an important theme for the foundation of polymer science. [4] Currently, many physical parameters of polymers still have to be characterized using their solutions, such as measuring the molecular weight and molecular weight distribution using gel permeation chromatography (GPC) and detecting the branching lever of polyolefins using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. The polarity parameters, α, β, and π*, are usually obtained using the so-called solvatochromic comparison method. [9,11,12] Polymers and ILs can be categorized as either H-bond acidic (α>β) or H-bond basic (α<β). First, the "complementary" requirement, i.e., one H-bond acidic component and another basic component, must be fulfilled to dissolve the polymer in a selected IL. Then, if the product of ΔαΔβ<0, where Δα = αp - αIL, and Δβ = βp - βIL, the IL usually exhibits satisfying solubility for the tested polymer. Strictly speaking, the change of hydrogen bonding interaction energy for the dissolving of polymer in an IL should be (Aαpβp + BαpβIL) - (CαILβp + DαILβIL), where A, B, C and D are coefficients according to Eq. (2). [10] However, the good correlation of ΔαΔβ = -[(αILβp + αpβIL) - (αpβp + αILβIL)] < 0 and the solubility of polymer/IL mixtures suggests that the simplified relationship, (αILβp + αpβIL) - (αpβp + αILβIL), can be used to approximately predict the change of hydrogen bonding interaction energy for the mixing of polymer/IL, i.e., ΔαΔβ<0 generally indicates that the hydrogen bonding interaction energy between the polymer and IL is higher than the hydrogen bonding interaction energy inside the components themselves. Because nonspecific (van der Waals) and polar interactions are commonly weaker than hydrogen bonding interactions in polymer/IL mixtures, QHB analysis (ΔαΔβ) provides a simple but reliable way to predict the sign of ΔHₘ (i.e., Xeff), and thus the solubility of a polymer/IL mixture. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are eutectic mixtures, typic-ally composed of hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs, e.g., qua-ternary ammonium salts, and aromatic alcohols) and hydro-gen bond donors (HBDs, e.g., carboxylic acids, amides, amines, and polyols) at certain stoichiometric ratios.[13–15] They are considered as "designer" solvents that are alterna-tives to ILs because they also exhibit negligible vapor pres-sures at room temperature, and their physico-chemical prop-erties can be fine-tuned by varying the starting HBA and HBD components or simply altering their molar ratios. They have extra advantages compared with ILs; for example, they do not need any solvent and special purification steps during syn-thesis, and they usually have low toxicity and cost, as the raw materials for preparation are usually nontoxic and abundant.[16] DESs, as new-generation solvents, show applica-tion potential in many fields of polymer sciences, such as polymer polymerization,[17] biomass fractionation,[18] and ion- ic soft materials. [19] Most of these applications involve the dis-solution of polymers in desired DESs. It is well accepted that hydrogen bonding plays an important role in the depression of melting points for HBA and HBD components and the formation of DESs. On that account, it is believed that the QHB analysis developed for polymer/IL mixtures can also work well for predicting the solubility of polymers in DESs. Here, the validity of QHB analysis was first evaluated by testing the solubility of carefully selected polymer/DES pairs. Then, attention was given to the solubility of cellulose in DESS because most DESs adopted to dissolve cellulose materials actually show no or very limited solubilities. [20-22] The QHB analysis based on hydrogen bonding interactions can provide a rational explanation. # RESULTS AND DISCUSSION ## Evaluating the Applicability of QHB Analysis for Polymer/DES Mixtures First, the applicability of QHB analysis for polymer/DES mixtures is evaluated by testing the solubilities of seven typical polymers in carefully selected DESs. The ηsp~c scaling rela- tionships for the PMMA/Thymol–OctA solutions are 1.05, 1.85, and 3.87 (Fig. S5 in ESI), which are close to the power laws of 1.0, 1.3, and 3.9 obtained for the neutral polymer in a good solvent.[42] Moreover, the ratio between entanglement con- centration, ce, and overlap concentration, c*, of PMMA/Thymol– OctA solutions is ~10 (Fig. S5 in ESI), and this is an important feature for polymer solutions in good solvents.[42,43] It has been realized that ILs are more dynamically heterogeneous than DESs with similar functionalities, which are due to the display of different intermolecular interactions within the constituent species.[44] The different solution dynamics between polymer/IL and polymer/DES also point to the fact that different heterogeneous microstructures and dynamics might exist in the two kinds of solutions. More experimental results are needed to explore this topic in the future. ## CONCLUSIONS The applicability of the newly developed QHB analysis based on the KAT polarity parameters for polymer/DES (the type III) was evaluated by testing the solubility of carefully selected polymer/DES pairs. The DES systems were chosen because it was generally accepted that hydrogen bonding interactions play an important role in the formation of DESs. Based on the dissolution results for all the tested polymer/DES pairs, it is concluded that (1) the "complementary" principle (one component H-bond acidic and the other basic) as a prerequisite has to be satisfied if a polymer can be expected to be dissolved in a desired DES. The "complementary" principle can help one to understand why many DESs exhibit very limited or no solubilities for cellulose materials in previous studies. This is because most of the DESs adopted in these studies have been of the H-bond acidic type. It is not surprising that cellulose, which is a kind of strong H-bond acidic polymer, cannot be dissolved in H-bond acidic DESs. (2) The QHB analysis works well for predicting the solubility of polymers in DESs. The H-bond basic DESs, which satisfy the criterion of ΔαΔβ<0, exhibit positive capacities for cellulose dissolution. The DES of MeaCl-DETA (1:4) can dissolve MCC at concentrations ranging between 2.0 wt% and 3.0 wt%. However, the superior solubility of cellulose (≥10 wt%), which is very common for typical H-bond basic ILs, is rarely observed for H-bond basic DESs. Two possible reasons for this are proposed: the number of hydrogen bonds formed between cellulose-DESs is less than that between cellulose-ILs, and the entropy gain for the dissolution of cellulose in ILs is higher than that for the dissolution process in DESs. In the future, more research is needed to delineate the in- fluences of the types, chemical structures, and molar ratios of HBA and HBD species on the KAT polarities of DESs. The first- principle-based COSMO-RS derived modeling approach has also been used to predict the KAT polarity scales of DESs.[45] It is believed that all these efforts will help to rapidly screen effi- cient DESs with the guidance of QHB analysis for the dissolu- tion of a specific polymer, including natural polymers, such as cellulose, lignin, chitin, and starch. ## NOTES The authors declare no competing financial interest. However, for PEO, its insolubility in the DESs formed by ChCl with GlyA and LevA, respectively, does not satisfy the criterion of ΔαΔβ<0, as (Δα, Δβ) are (-0.49, 0.15) and (-0.51, 0.08) for two PEO/DES pairs. It can be found that the two Δβ values are relatively small. Considering that the used KAT parameters are adopted from different references and are obtained by using different solvatochromic probes, an uncertainty of 0.1 or even more for KAT parameters is very possible. [11] This is an unavoidable limitation of the solvatochromic comparison method. The accuracy of the QHB analysis is mainly determined by the accuracy of KAT parameters adopted. As a suggestion, it is better to use KAT parameters measured using the same sets of solvatochromic probes to ensure the predictive accuracy of QHB analysis. Taking the possible uncertainties of KAT parameters into account, the insolubility of PEO in these two solvents is acceptable even as the QHB analysis predicts the solubility. On the other hand, for all the tested H-bond acidic polymer/H-bond acidic DES pairs, none are soluble regardless of whether or not the criterion of ΔαΔβ<0 is satisfied. All these results suggest that the "complementary" principle of solubility (one component H-bond acidic and the other basic) we have previ- ously found in polymer/IL mixtures [6] is also well applicable for the polymer/DES mixtures studied here, while the H-bond neutral DESs can be considered to exhibit duality, i.e., they can be treated as either H-bond acidic or H-bond basic. For all 13 pairs of H-bond basic polymer/H-bond acidic DES examined here (Table S2 in ESI), only two pairs violate the proposed ΔαΔβ criterion. One is PEO/ChCl-EG (insoluble), and the other is PVAc/menthol-LevA (soluble). The values of (Δα, Δβ) for the two mixtures are (-1.47, 0.08) (soluble as predicted) and (-1.56, -0.18) (insoluble as predicted), respectively. The failure to predict solubility can also be ascribed to the uncertainty in the adopted KAT parameters. When we tried to seek H-bond basic DESs, it was found that they are evidently less than the H-bond acidic DESs. In a typical DES, the molar percentage of the HBD component is commonly equal to or higher than that of HBA. Moreover, the HBA component is usually an organic salt, which can also be considered to be composed of HBA (anion) and HBD (cation) components. Thus, there are more functional groups inside a DES that can play the role of proton donors, and thus, it is prone to exhibit as H-bond acidic, which embodies a relatively high α value. Although some research works have been carried out to systemically study the influence of the types, chemical structures, and molar ratios of HBA and HBD on the polarities of different families of DESs, a general and detailed delineation has not been obtained at present. The DES systems were chosen because it was generally accepted that hydrogen bonding interactions play an important role in the formation of DESs. Based on the dissolution results for all the tested polymer/DES pairs, it is concluded that (1) the "complementary" principle (one component H-bond acidic and the other basic) as a prerequisite has to be satisfied if a polymer can be expected to be dissolved in a desired DES. The "complementary" principle can help one to understand why many DESs exhibit very limited or no solubilities for cellulose materials in previous studies. This is because most of the DESs adopted in these studies have been of the H-bond acidic type. It is not surprising that cellulose, which is a kind of strong H-bond acidic polymer, cannot be dissolved in H-bond acidic DESs. (2) The QHB analysis works well for predicting the solubility of polymers in DESs. The H-bond basic DESs, which satisfy the criterion of ΔαΔβ<0, exhibit positive capacities for cellulose dissolution. The DES of MeaCl-DETA (1:4) can dissolve MCC at concentrations ranging between 2.0 wt% and 3.0 wt%. However, the superior solubility of cellulose (≥10 wt%), which is very common for typical H-bond basic ILs, is rarely observed for H-bond basic DESs. Two possible reasons for this are proposed: the number of hydrogen bonds formed between cellulose-DESs is less than that between cellulose-ILs, and the entropy gain for the dissolution of cellulose in ILs is higher than that for the dissolution process in DESs. In the future, more research is needed to delineate the in- fluences of the types, chemical structures, and molar ratios of HBA and HBD species on the KAT polarities of DESs. The first- principle-based COSMO-RS derived modeling approach has also been used to predict the KAT polarity scales of DESs.[45] It is believed that all these efforts will help to rapidly screen effi- cient DESs with the guidance of QHB analysis for the dissolu- tion of a specific polymer, including natural polymers, such as cellulose, lignin, chitin, and starch. ## NOTES The authors declare no competing financial interest.
